method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0) 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines' (published 5 June 2024), 22 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11723931). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)' (retrieved 24 September 2026), 8 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC 4.0. eviQ also states that its content should not be hosted on external sites, and that commercial entities must contact eviQ to seek permission (https://www.eviq.org.au/copyright). Adaptations must cite the eviQ ID, version and URL. (read at https://www.eviq.org.au/copyright (Disclaimer and copyright page)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, four Australian eviQ GIST treatment protocols (paraphrased and hash-anchored), for Australian dosing, PBS-linked dose limits, the ripretinib line of therapy and TKI monitoring. The S2 source file concatenates https://www.eviq.org.au/p/1222, /p/330, /p/329 and /p/4112, each under a header line naming its URL. eviQ's regorafenib protocol (1902) is marked superseded and was not used. S1 claims and fragments are unchanged.

claims.claim: **Typical presentations:** upper GI bleeding and anaemia; larger tumours cause pain or a mass. Small-bowel GISTs can stay silent until they bleed or rupture.
claims.source_text: The most common symptoms of GIST include upper gastrointestinal bleeding and anaemia, whilst larger tumours may present with abdominal pain/discomfort and a palpable mass. Small bowel GISTs may remain silent for a long period before presenting with an acute event such as haemorrhage or rupture.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Investigate and diagnose any suspected GIST over 2 cm**, usually by EUS biopsy in the stomach, duodenum or rectum. Incidental lesions under 2 cm need no routine surveillance.
claims.source_text: Suspected GISTs larger than 2 cm in diameter should be investigated and a diagnosis made whenever possible. Often this can be done by EUS biopsy, provided the lesion is in the stomach, duodenum, or rectum. [IVC] … Incidental small, i.e. <2 cm lesions do not require routine surveillance
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis needs an experienced pathologist**, with CD117 and/or DOG1 immunohistochemistry and molecular testing where needed; about 1% of GISTs stain for neither.
claims.source_text: The diagnosis of GIST should be established by a pathologist experienced in the disease and should include the use of IHC and, if necessary, molecular analysis (which should be performed by an accredited laboratory). [IVC] … about 1% of GISTs are immunonegative for both
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Confirm the diagnosis and genotype before imatinib.** Some GISTs, notably PDGFRA exon 18 D842V, are insensitive to TKIs.
claims.source_text: If initial treatment with imatinib is planned, it is essential to confirm the diagnosis of GIST, since there is a wide differential [IVC]. It may be necessary to perform a percutaneous core needle biopsy if the tumour is inaccessible to EUS biopsy. Molecular analysis is particularly critical, since some GISTs are insensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. the PDGFRA exon 18 D842V mutation). [IIB]
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **KIT/PDGFRA mutation analysis at minimum for:** resected moderate- or high-risk or ruptured tumours, biopsies before neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy, unresectable or metastatic disease, and suspected syndromic GIST.
claims.source_text: as a minimum, such analysis should be performed on all the following specimens: resected moderate or high-risk GISTs at any site; resected GISTs showing tumour rupture; biopsies diagnostic of GIST prior to neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy; specimens from patients with unresectable and/or metastatic GIST; GISTs which are suspected to be syndromic.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For KIT/PDGFRA wild-type GIST not linked to NF1**, do SDHB immunohistochemistry, then test for BRAF/RAS and finally NTRK fusions, which are rare but targetable.
claims.source_text: For KIT/PDGFRA WT GISTs which are not NF1-related, IHC for succinate dehydrogenase B (SDHB) should be performed if available since loss of expression may assist the diagnosis and may help guide therapy. Further molecular analysis may demonstrate a loss of functional variant in a SDH gene or epigenetic loss, usually in SDHC. KIT/PDGFRA WT GISTs which do not show SDHB loss should then be analysed for BRAF and RAS variants; BRAF variants are especially important to exclude as they may be targeted therapeutically. Finally, GISTs which are WT for KIT, PDGFRA and BRAF/RAS and show no SDH-deficiency or NF1 association should be interrogated for NTRK fusions. GISTs with NTRK fusions are very rare but are potential candidates for TRK inhibitor therapy.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prognosis rests on mitotic rate, tumour size and site**; gastric GISTs do better than small-bowel or rectal ones, and rupture is adverse and must be recorded. TNM staging is not recommended.
claims.source_text: The TNM classification does not add to existing prognostic systems for GIST and its use is not recommended in this disease. Prognostic factors of proven value are the mitotic rate, tumour size and tumour site. Gastric GISTs have a better prognosis than small bowel or rectal GISTs. Tumour rupture through a serosal surface is an adverse prognostic factor and should be recorded, whether it took place before or during surgery.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stage with contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis**; MRI is better for rectal GIST and an option in younger patients to limit radiation.
claims.source_text: Contrast-enhanced abdominal and pelvic CT scan is the investigation of choice for staging and follow-up. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or contrast-enhanced ultrasound may be alternatives, especially in younger patients where exposure to radiation should be limited. MRI provides better preoperative staging information for rectal GISTs.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Standard treatment is complete (R0, margin at least 1 mm) excision without dissecting clinically negative nodes**, by a trained cancer surgeon in or linked to a specialist centre. Avoid rupture: it carries a very high relapse risk.
claims.source_text: Standard treatment of localised GIST is complete excision to achieve an R0 resection, i.e. ≥1 mm, if possible, with no dissection of clinically negative lymph nodes [IIIA]. Surgery should be performed by an appropriately trained cancer surgeon either in, or linked to, a specialist centre. This also applies to laparoscopic or robotic excision [IIIA]. … Specific attention must be taken to avoid tumour rupture during resection as this is associated with a very high risk of relapse.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider neoadjuvant imatinib when R0 surgery would need total gastrectomy or abdominoperineal resection**, provided the genotype is sensitive. Operate at maximal response, generally after 6-9 months; stop imatinib about a week before surgery.
claims.source_text: If a total gastrectomy or abdominoperineal resection would be required to achieve an R0 resection consideration should be given to neoadjuvant therapy with imatinib, provided the tumour is not driven by a drug-resistant variant, e.g. PDGFRA exon 18 D842V mutation. … it is usually stopped a week before surgery … Typically, surgery is performed after maximal tumour response, generally after 6-9 months of neo-adjuvant treatment.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adjuvant imatinib for 3 years is standard for high-risk resected GIST** with a sensitive driver (e.g. KIT exon 11); 3 years beat 1 year for relapse-free and overall survival.
claims.source_text: Adjuvant treatment with imatinib for 3 years was associated with improved relapse-free and overall survival compared with 1 year of therapy in a randomised trial in high-risk patients … Therefore, adjuvant therapy with imatinib for 3 years is standard treatment for patients with a high risk of relapse and a potentially sensitive driver variant, e.g. KIT exon 11.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **No adjuvant imatinib for PDGFRA D842V or NF1-related GIST.** An R1 margin alone is not an indication if the tumour is otherwise not high risk; SDH-deficient GIST has no agreed approach.
claims.source_text: There is a consensus that PDGFRA D842V-mutant GISTs should not be treated with adjuvant therapy, given the lack of sensitivity of this genotype to imatinib. … There is consensus on avoiding adjuvant treatment in NF-1 related GISTs, which are insensitive to imatinib in the advanced setting. … Marginal excision, i.e. an R1 resection, is not in itself an indication for adjuvant therapy if the tumour is otherwise not high risk. … a consensus is lacking among experts about whether KIT/PDGFRA WT, SDH-deficient GIST should be treated with adjuvant therapy
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After tumour rupture, assume occult peritoneal disease** and give adjuvant imatinib for at least 3 years, probably for life.
claims.source_text: If there has been tumour rupture before or during surgery, there will have been spillage of tumour cells into the peritoneal cavity and therefore occult peritoneal disease can be assumed to exist. This puts the patient at a very high risk of peritoneal relapse. Therefore, these patients should be considered for adjuvant imatinib therapy. The optimal duration of treatment in these cases is unknown, given the uncertainty as to whether they should be viewed as having essentially metastatic disease, but should be at least 3 years, as for high risk resected GIST, and probably life-long.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Australian adjuvant imatinib (eviQ):** 400 mg by mouth once daily for up to 3 years, started after recovery and within 3 months of surgery, for primary GIST at high risk of relapse, defined as over 5 cm with more than 5 mitoses per 50 HPF, over 10 cm at any mitotic rate, or more than 10 mitoses per 50 HPF.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **First line: imatinib 400 mg daily, continued indefinitely until progression.** For KIT exon 9 mutations, 800 mg daily improves PFS (and survival in long-term follow-up); not for PDGFRA D842V.
claims.source_text: The standard dose of imatinib is 400 mg daily. However, data have shown that patients with KIT exon 9 variants fare better in terms of progression-free survival (PFS) on a higher dose of 800 mg daily, which is therefore the standard treatment in this subgroup []. A report on the long-term follow-up of the European / Australasian clinical trial which compared 400 mg with 800 mg imatinib in patients with advanced GIST has shown a significant survival advantage for the initial use of the 800 mg dose in those with KIT exon 9 variants with a hazard ratio of 0.54 … Treatment should be continued indefinitely, since treatment interruption is generally followed by relatively rapid tumour progression … Imatinib is not recommended for patients with PDGFRA exon 18 D842V mutant disease [IC].
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Support adherence:** explain drug and food interactions (especially grapefruit, a CYP3A4 inhibitor), and manage side-effects to keep dose intensity.
claims.source_text: At the start of treatment, the patient should be alerted to the importance of adherence to therapy, and of possible interactions with concomitant medications and foods, especially grapefruit, a potent inhibitor of the liver enzyme CYP3A4. … Dose intensity should be maintained by effective management of side effects, and a rational policy of dose reductions and interruptions should be applied if there is excessive, persistent toxicity.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Second line: sunitinib**, 50 mg daily for 4 weeks in every 6, or 37.5 mg daily continuously.
claims.source_text: Standard second line treatment is sunitinib, which may be given at the recommended dose of 50 mg daily for 4 weeks every 6 weeks, or 37.5 mg daily continuously [IA].
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Later lines:** regorafenib (160 mg daily, 3 weeks on/1 off) is the UK third-line standard. Ripretinib after 3 or more TKIs gave median PFS 6.3 v 1.0 months and median OS 15.1 v 6.6 months against placebo, but did not beat sunitinib in second line.
claims.source_text: Regorafenib is regarded as standard therapy for the third-line treatment of patients progressing on imatinib and sunitinib. A prospective placebo-controlled randomised trial demonstrated that regorafenib, at a dose of 160 mg daily on a 3 weeks on/1 week off schedule … who had progressed after treatment with 3 or more TKIs. … The median PFS on ripretinib was 6.3 months (95% CI: 4.6, 6.9) compared with 1.0 month (95% CI: 0.9, 1.7) on placebo. The median OS ripretinib arm was 15.1 months (95% CI: 12.3, 15.1) compared with 6.6 months … A clinical trial comparing ripretinib with sunitinib after treatment with imatinib failed to show an improvement in PFS overall
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PDGFRA D842V: avapritinib is the most active drug** (300 mg daily; 79% partial and 9% complete responses in the phase I study).
claims.source_text: The trial concluded that a dose of 300 mg daily was safe and tolerable. In patients with PDGFRA exon 18 D842V mutations there were 49 of 56 responses, with 44 partial responses (79%) and five complete responses (9%) … Avapritinib remains the most active treatment for PDGFRA D842V mutant GIST.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Limited progression** (such as a 'nodule within a mass') may suit surgery, RFA or radiotherapy while continuing the TKI; surgery for generalised progression is not recommended. Offer trials to all with advanced disease.
claims.source_text: Isolated progression may be amenable to surgery or other local measures, such as radiofrequency ablation [IVB]. … Surgical excision of progressive disease is not recommended, given the poor results in published series, but surgery or ablation of limited progression, such as the 'nodule within a mass', has been associated with a progression-free interval in the same range as for second-line treatment with sunitinib. So, this may be a palliative option in the individual patient with limited progression, while continuing imatinib. … It is important that all patients with advanced disease be considered for participation in clinical trials when available
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Judge response on size and density together.** A tumour can grow briefly yet be responding if CT density falls; new enhancement inside a responding low-density lesion may signal progression. Have an experienced team confirm early progression.
claims.source_text: Response assessment is complex and early progression should be confirmed by a team experienced in treating GIST. … Tumour size may even increase in the short term but if tumour density on CT scan is decreased this may still indicate tumour response … an increase in the tumour density shown by contrast enhancement within a previously responding low density tumour lesion, may be indicative of tumour progression.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Australian imatinib dose ceiling:** in metastatic or unresectable GIST, keep responders on 400 mg daily and reassess regularly; non-responders may go up to 600 mg daily. eviQ notes that PBS Authority applications for more than 600 mg a day will not be approved.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Imatinib monitoring:** baseline TSH, FBC, EUC, eGFR and LFTs; FBC weekly in month one, fortnightly in month two, then every 2 to 3 months; LFTs monthly. Watch for fluid retention and periorbital oedema (withhold if severe), and check LVEF at baseline if there is heart disease.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Sunitinib in Australia is second line** for KIT (CD117)-positive advanced GIST after imatinib failure or intolerance: 50 mg daily for 4 weeks then 2 weeks off (42-day cycle). With a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, lower the dose in 12.5 mg steps to no less than 25 mg; with a CYP3A4 inducer, raise it in 12.5 mg steps to no more than 87.5 mg.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Sunitinib safety:** control blood pressure before starting, then check it weekly for 6 weeks and regularly after; withhold for severe or uncontrolled hypertension. Arrange a dental review before treatment and every 6 months (jaw osteonecrosis risk). Bloods at baseline, week 2 and 4-weekly; thyroid function every 8 to 12 weeks.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ripretinib in Australia follows imatinib and sunitinib:** for metastatic or unresectable GIST after failure of, or intolerance to, both, with ECOG 0 to 2. Dose 150 mg (three 50 mg tablets) once daily until progression or unacceptable toxicity, reducing to 100 mg daily if needed; stop if 100 mg cannot be tolerated or a delay exceeds 4 weeks.
claims.locator: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online, Cancer Institute NSW, 'eviQ GIST protocols (protocols, not guidelines): 1222 'GIST adjuvant imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 330 'GIST metastatic imatinib' (v.7, review as required), 329 'GIST metastatic sunitinib' (v.7, review as required) and 4112 'GIST metastatic ripretinib' (v.3, first approved 13 May 2022, review due 31 December 2027)', retrieved 24 September 2026, https://www.eviq.org.au/medical-oncology/upper-gastrointestinal/gastrointestinal-stromal-cell-tumours, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Ripretinib raises the risk of new skin cancers** (squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, melanoma): examine the skin at the start and routinely during treatment. Hand-foot syndrome and rash usually appear in the first 6 weeks. Bloods fortnightly in the first month, then 4-weekly.

claims.claim: **For any TKI, assess the heart at baseline** (ECG and biochemistry, especially with cardiovascular disease; echocardiogram if high risk), repeat when clinically indicated or when a QT-prolonging drug is started, and interrupt treatment around major surgery until the wound has healed.

claims.claim: **High risk on adjuvant therapy:** cross-sectional imaging every 3-6 months for the first 3 years, then 3-monthly for 2 years after stopping, 6-monthly for 3 years, then yearly for at least 5 years. High-risk patients not given adjuvant therapy follow the post-adjuvant schedule.
claims.source_text: Patients with high risk disease on adjuvant therapy should be followed up with cross-sectional imaging every 3-6 months during their first 3 years of treatment, 3 monthly for 2 years following cessation of treatment and thereafter every 6 months for 3 years and then annually for at least 5 years. [IVC] Patients with high risk disease not receiving adjuvant treatment should follow the post-adjuvant surveillance scheme. [IVC]
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intermediate risk:** 6-monthly scans for 5 years then yearly is reasonable, though perhaps unnecessary. **Low risk:** consider yearly CT or ultrasound for 5 years and watch for second cancers. **Very low risk:** no routine surveillance.
claims.source_text: For intermediate risk patients, according to AFIP criteria, 6 monthly scans for 5 years followed by annual scans is considered reasonable, but may be unnecessary according to some recent reports. The optimum duration of follow-up is unknown. [IVC] In low risk GIST the role of routine surveillance imaging is unclear. Annual CT or USS for 5 years may be considered and clinical follow-up to check for a second malignancy is sensible, given the high frequency of second tumours in this disease. [IVC] Very low risk patients do not require routine surveillance. [IVC]
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02672-0), 'Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST): British Sarcoma Group clinical practice guidelines', published 5 June 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11723931/, retrieved 2026-09-23
